utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm listening on channel 1, so I am listening to him in the original, and the translation is incorrect where it says he said "Military District." So I don't know how you wish to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you say it is incorrect, you suggest that we should look at it and see whether it was correct because you have doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't have any doubts, but can you take a look at it, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But the way in which we address our interpreters is that you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Your Honour. I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not that you can tell the interpreters that they made a mistake, but that you heard in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just a matter of the manner in how we deal, and there's no problem in raising any translation issue. But we invite them, just to see whether they come to the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me be clear. I wish to apologise. It was not my intention to be rude, but the particular issue here is that there's a specific military term in the Croatian system that is being used that may not be familiar to everyone. I point it out, and in no way did I intend to suggest anything improper. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that your apologies are accepted. Now, Mr. Misetic, if could you take me back to the line exactly where --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page 48, Mr. President, at line 10 -- line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 11. Yes. First of all, there is some doubts. Could the interpreters if they say, Well, Mr. Misetic is right, then we could deal with it right away; if not, we'll ask the witness to repeat his words. Could I hear from the English booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am or the interpreters are not exactly sure what Mr. Misetic is referring to exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is referring to page 48, line 11, where it was translated "the Military District doctor." Mr. Misetic, could you tell us what you heard in the original, so that we first establish whether you heard the same as the interpreters did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, "Military District" in Croatian is "Zborno Podrucje," the "Garrison" is "Zborno Mjesto," and I believe the witness said "Zborno Mjesto."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which would be in line with what we find under the remarks, yes. Could the interpreters already clarify the issue; otherwise, we'll ask the witness to repeat his words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure what it was exactly that they heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will ask the witness again. Could you please put your earphones on again, Mr. Dzolic? Mr. Dzolic, you earlier said - and I leave out the words which are in dispute - you said: "In other words," and then you refer to a doctor, apparently attached to some institution, was probably supposed to get in touch with his technical service. Could you again tell us what doctor or to institution the doctor was attached as referred to in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The doctor, this medical service, existed there. It was in the units of the armed forces, but also it was logical then, as far as I can remember, that the same kind of professional was also at a higher level of command, who was an assistant to the commander in this sphere of work or in this purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said "there." We're looking at where exactly. Perhaps I put it to you: Did you refer to the doctor of the Military District, or did you refer to a doctor of the Garrison? What did you refer to: Doctor, Military District; or doctor of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I mentioned the garrison. I think my reference was to the garrison. However, if I take a better look at this report, or this paragraph, where it says the report for the Military District of Knin, and I wasn't able to get in touch with a doctor over the phone, I allow that it is possible that the Knin area of responsibility was -- or Military District -- or, rather, the garrison of Knin was -- received this report, and then someone from the garrison referred them to the doctor who was in charge of sanitization of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the witness has explained what he intended to say. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in instances like this, where the doctor of the garrison was required for sanitization of bodies, where would they, the military police -- or which section of the garrison would they contact? Was there a duty service of the garrison? What point would they contact?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, questions have to be asked -- shall we find out if there were other situations, rather than it being in situations like this. Shall we try and establish that any procedure that there may be in ways that the witness can give his own evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't see anything improper in that question, Mr. President, but to save time I will phrase it so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, if you needed to obtain the services of the doctor that you have been talking about all this time, where would you call in the garrison?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: What would I need the doctor for?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm saying in a scenario, if you needed a doctor to, let's say, sanitize bodies or with regard to the disposal of bodies, where would you call?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: The doctor in charge of those tasks, the competent doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I know. But did he have an individual telephone or would you call a particular section within the garrison? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Probably, I didn't manage to get him on the phone. There was a phone. Someone had the telephone number of the doctor whose duty this was, and he was a doctor that had to be called. But who the doctor actually was, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is no answer to your question. What Ms. Mahindaratne was trying to find out was not who actually the doctor was that was tried to be reached; but in such circumstances as depicted by Ms. Mahindaratne, would you just choose any doctor or would you choose to phone to a specific department of the garrison? Was there any procedure established how to get hold of a doctor for sanitization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, there was a procedure. A procedure did exist for the sanitization of the terrain. What the procedure was, I'm not aware; and, probably, the leader of the duty service who was on duty at the time wasn't aware of it either. He informed the garrison of the event that had happened in the area of responsibility, and he probably received guidance from them as to what doctor he should call and at what telephone number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you understand it to be the task of the garrison to coordinate or give guidance in this type of situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours, what the garrison's task was in this respect. But in the course of my stay in Knin, in the time I spent there, I learned that sanitization of the terrain was carried out, that it was carried out by the civilian protection which was part of the Ministry of Interior. Probably, there should have been a person in the garrison who would monitor or coordinate the work with the sanitization team, if this had to do with a military facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzolic, did you at any time prior to Operation Storm receive instructions as to how to -- or as to what steps to take when the military police came across bodies of persons killed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I received no instructions about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And moving on, if could you move to the entry for 12th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that would be on B/C/S page 4, Mr. Registrar; and on the English page, it is 7452, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzolic, this is the duty log for 12th August; and, in fact, you would see at 11.45, you are indicated as providing some information. So you were there as a company commander. I'd like to you lock at entry at 10.15. There is a reference to: Senior Lieutenant," and the name is not too legible, "Pavlimovic informing the duty service that the building next to the barracks is on fire." Then the action taken is that the Ministry of Interior informed MUP informed which sent the fire brigades. Do you recall this incident, the building next to the barracks being on fire?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What I'm try to say is: Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall what the building which was next to the barracks? Was it a shop or a residential premises?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that. It doesn't even say next to which barracks. There were two or three barracks in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this log-book, there is no record of what investigations had been carried out as to the cause of the fire. Now, can you tell us, you were the company commander so you should know, if there was a fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection to the leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic. Yes. Whether he should know, Ms. Mahindaratne, depends on many circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please refrain from including this kind of, could I say, encouragements to give an answer as you would expect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Unfortunately, I don't think I have the capacity to lead this witness at all, even if it was permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is another comment, Ms. Mahindaratne, which does not assist the Chamber in trying to understand the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzolic, if you could just, say, tell us, if information was received about a fire, what would you, as company commander, do? What instructions would you issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going object because it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact Ms. Mahindaratne, although she started her questioning by specific reference to the entry in the log-book, her question is now is a very general one: If a fire would be reported, what would you do? Then, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can I make a comment if he takes his earphones off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take your earphones off for a second? Mr. Dzolic, could you take your earphones off?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the mixing of the specifics and then broadening out to a general, A, confuses the witness; B, the specific remark is that MUP was informed. So is she asking him what he would expect as a commander of the military police after a matter was referred to the MUP? Is she asking him what would he except if a fire was committed within a military barracks by it? I mean, it is an overly broad question that's tied to a specific entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point. Ms. Mahindaratne, it came into my mind earlier when we say "the building next to the barracks is on fire," of course, the witness now said he doesn't even know what barracks, but I was trying to imagine what you were asking for. Now I see military barracks which is usually, well, a complex of buildings, structures. And now there is "the building next to the barracks." Is that south, west, east, and north? Then you asked, were these shops, or I think you asked whether it was civilian houses, something like that. Whatever the witness would answer, he could not possibly answer that question in a reliable way without further information about - had not even thought about what barracks - but at least what side "the building." I've never seen a barracks with only one building next to it, or it is at least two. But if we're talking about Knin barracks, whether it would be northern barracks or any other barracks, I would know on the basis of a map, that there's a likelihood that there at least ten, 15, if not 20, or we have seen pictures earlier of some barracks with houses around it. That is a question which almost impossibly could lead to any useful information without further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will move on, Mr. President. I will use the next entry which is far more clearer, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And then Mr. Misetic asked you always to make a clear distinction between questions focussing on the entry and questions which were not exclusively related to that entry anymore. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do that. Mr. President. It's just that following the objection, I moved on to the generality from the specifics. That's what happened. But I will now move on to -- -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you said "another entry, so there the same problem might arise. I am not saying will arise, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, we are not talking about that entry anymore. I would like to ask you a general question. If you, as company commander, received information of a fire, you know, of some structures on fire within your area of responsibility, what would you do as a company commander?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Well, probably what it says here, what this Officer Pavlimovic did. I would report to the duty service, and they would, if this was a civilian building, inform the Ministry of Interior; that is, the civilian police. If the fire was on a military facility, they would send a patrol of the military police, and they would probably also call the fire-fighters to come and put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if this was a civilian building, after the fire was put out, would there be an investigation into the cause of the fire?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Well, if it was military facility and if it was with a discovered or if there was information that a member of the armed forces had committed the crime of arson, then a criminal investigation would be started. If there was no information as to the cause of the fire, there would be no investigation because there would be no perpetrator, or a criminal report would be filed against an unknown perpetrator. If it was a military facility, a military police patrol would be sent to secure the site, and then the crime investigation military police would be sent to carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What if it was a civilian facility and there was information that the perpetrators were members of the armed forces -- sorry, members of the military, would the same process be followed as you just said?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: If there was information that the perpetrators of the crime were members of the Croatian army who were not in the barracks or the military facilities, then the military police and the civilian police would jointly carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if there was an investigation, would this -- or if a criminal report was raised, would your duty log indicate that fact?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Probably, it would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I'm going to make a late objection as to the compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That last question, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two parts to the question, so I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Two parts based on the witness's answer. I just read back what he said and then asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you read back. The question was: "If there was an investigation or if a criminal report was raised, would your duty log indicate that fact?" I'm saying it's a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Because the previous answer was dealing with the military police and civilian police would jointly carry out an investigation, and then my question was: "If there was an investigation or if a criminal ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if we start with "if there was an investigation, would your duty log indicate that fact," and then go to the other possibility, apparently, because you said "if this or if that happened, would it be recorded."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I will move on, Mr. President. I think the question has been answered anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the problem is that if the question is compound and if the answer does not make the distinction which should be made in order to fully understand the answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, President. I will ask him a further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, your answer to my question as to whether the duty log would indicate it is -- you say "Probably, it would ..." -- it is recorded as: "Probably, it would be recorded." And when you said, "Probably, it would be recorded," could you specify --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection as to the leading now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just said could you specify. What is the leading part of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I could explain to you what is apparently what Mr. Misetic is saying. Why not ask: "If such an investigation as you referred to, if that investigation was a joint investigation by the military and the civilian police, would such an investigation be recorded in the log-book or somewhere else?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, could you answer the question from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: It would be recorded in the log-book, the duty log-book, the log-book of the leader of the duty shift, as a piece of information on the event --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the duty officer had information from the duty service that there had been a joint investigation carried out, this would be recorded in the duty service log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if this would result in a criminal report, would that be recorded; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information would be entered into the duty log-book. If there had been a patrol going out on the ground, they would draw up their own separate report, which would then be sent as a separate report to the superior command. The crime investigation military police never sent all the information whether a criminal report had been filed or not. They would only provide the basic information that a perpetrator had been discovered and that he was being investigated. In the duty log, only this information would be recorded: The crime investigation military police is dealing with the case, and the case is under way; or if it has been completed, it's been referred to the military court or whatever. Whatever happened would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So only the basic information would be recorded in the log-book; whereas, the report as such was further submitted to the competent authorities to further decide on the matter. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crime investigation military police would carry out their own procedure, and they would forward this to the military court. As for the information concerning the event, the duty service would draw up a separate report, as information, and forward it to their superior professional body, which would be the battalion duty service, and they would forward it to the military police administration. So it would be a separate report, stating that this event had occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that investigation took place and whether, for example, someone was arrested, would that find its way in the log-book, this basic information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If someone had been brought in to the military police unit, as I said before, they would be brought to the duty service and that would be recorded along with the basic information in the daily log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just for my information, if people were sent and if a joint investigation would have -- You apparently have problems with the earphones. Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a joint investigation would have taken place without anyone arrested, without clear conclusions as, for example, the cause of fire, would that then be reported back and would that information also find its way into the log-book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If an incident occurred, that information would be recorded; but if there was no information about the perpetrator of the crime, there would be nothing to enter into the log-book, the duty log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move to page, on B/C/S, page 26; on English, 7472, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzolic, if you could just like at the entry for 31st August 1995, at 1205, there is -- there is information from, it says, "Matas Forward Command Post." Are you able to say what that is? What forward command post is that information coming from? Perhaps you can read the entire entry for at that time-period and offer an explanation. From which forward command post is that information coming?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Forward command post or separate command post? That's how I would interpret this. I don't see what this is about, what the incident is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, I'm not asking you to comment on the incident. I just asked you if you are able to recognise what the source of that information. Perhaps, there is an translation issue. What do you read in the B/C/S record as that information coming from?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: It says "Matas IZM." I don't know what that is, I don't know who this person is, or what this is supposed to be. I cannot draw a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Maybe if I knew what the incident involved was, I could then make a assumption to what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now that "IZM" - correct me if I'm wrong - is abbreviation for "Forward Command Post." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Probably, that's what it might mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, you are familiar with the abbreviations used in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object now. There has been no foundation. We are now on 31 August. There is no foundation established. The witness has now said in three answers he is making assumption. He might know what it means, he has now answered the "IZM" question, and now we're going at him again to say -- to challenge whether he should know it. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is also a compound objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think, even if it is late August, Ms. Mahindaratne can ask questions like, "Do you recognise the abbreviation 'IZM?'" I can imagine that if this is a standing abbreviation, that the parties could even try it agree on that. I've got no idea. But the witness said that he apparently does not know what "Matas" stands for. Perhaps, we could ask the question in a different way. Mr. Dzolic, Ms. Mahindaratne suggested to you what "IZM" would stand for. Apparently, you hesitated to agree with her. This, apparently, is an abbreviation. First question: Are you familiar with an abbreviation, "IZM"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does it stand for, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Separate Command Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. And if you would come to further explore what happened on the 31st of August, you will certainly remind the earlier observations made by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, in the information, it is recorded that: "On the orders of General Cermak, tapes with the military police sign should be placed on both sides of the road in front of the IZM to stop vehicles from parking." Then the remarks are that: "Military patrol, Mosor 31, has been informed and will place the tape." Now, my question is this: If I could take to you paragraph 45 of your 2004 statement, you refer to General Cermak, and you say: "I was called to Cermak's office like this on two or three occasions. The next time was 9th August 1995," and then you go on to describe the meeting. Now, my question is this: Would that, the fact that you were called into Mr. Cermak's office on thee occasions as indicated by you in your 2004 statement, be recorded in the duty log-book for that period?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Because I was invited by General Cermak to come there for a conversation because I was subordinate to him in the daily tasks. In other words, I did not report on everything that I did in the log, in the duty service log. The duty service log was for incidents that occurred in the field, on the ground. If I were to report on every move I made and where I went, then this log-book would have 500 pages or more, because it wouldn't just be me but every other commander who would have to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I asked you that question, Mr. Dzolic, because this really -- this is doesn't relate to an incident but just merely placing tapes, so that is why I asked you whether all such entries were, in fact, included in the duty log; and your response is no. Let me go on. Now, if I could take to you B/C/S page 28 and the English 7476, page 1. Now, Mr. Dzolic, I'm going to just go through a few entries with you, and then I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. To save time, I'll first take you through the entries. On this page, at 2140, there is a report from military police patrol, Mosor 198, to the shift leader, and the information is that: "They had," that's military police, "had stopped an HV truck with 40 sheep for which they had no papers." The action taken is: "M-31 patrol sent which took the persons in and handed them over to the crime police for criminal processing. They were released." I'd like to you go on -- this is for 1st and 2nd September, 3rd September. That is page B/C/S 29; English 7477, page 2. That is the entry for 3rd September 1995, and there are three entries which I will read to you. At 1410, there is name Denis Keljalj, VP, military police, informs shift leader personally: "The HV had been stopped at Kistanje KBP roadblock with stolen goods." The action taken is: "Patrol sent which brought in HV, handed them over to crime inspector, Runje," I think that is the area where you were based in, "and released them." The next entry, at 1620, the information comes from the Knin military police company commander at this stage, since you were not there, Luka Orsulic. The entry is: "The HV was steeling goods from a house near the Tvik company and was loading them into a lorry." Action taken: "Patrol sent which brought them in and handed them over to the Crime Police, Runje. They were released by the crime police." Third entry for the 3rd September, 1650, again from company commander himself: "The HV is supposed to come with a lorry to the round about," and time is given as 4.55 hours, "with stolen goods. Patrol sent, they were brought in, and handed over to criminal investigator, Runje, and released." I would like you to move on to the entry for 5th September; and that is at B/C/S page 32, and English translation 7480, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, do you notice an entry there for 5th September? This is 1625, where the Knin police station informs someone in the -- I think this is the shift leader, Vrkic: "The hospital is on fire and HV members are not letting firemen extinguish the fire." Action taken: Mosor patrol went personally to intervene and did not encounter the HV soldiers." I just go through two more -- before that, let me ask you, now, in these entries that I read back to you, there is no record of a criminal report being raised or the matter being investigated or the perpetrators being charged. In fact, in the cases of the looting incidents that I read back to you, it says that the perpetrators were released. Now, are you aware as to during time - I appreciate you left on 12th - but during this period, what action the Knin military police took with regard to perpetrators who were caught with looting or incidents where there was information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I think it would be appropriate, where you refer to some instances where the persons that were brought in were released, whether the witness has any personal knowledge either on specific cases or on a general attitude by the military police, in this period of time, in how to handle persons who were brought in on a suspicion of having looted. That's first what we should establish before we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, first and foremost, let me ask you, are you aware of those incidents that I read back to you where the persons were released or do you know what really happened?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, nor do I know of these events, these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What were the instruction that the military police had been given with regard to how you were supposed to act in the cases when suspected perpetrators of looting were brought in or apprehended?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I have to make an objection again. I'm sorry to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can ask the witness whether he is aware of instructions, and then, of course, we then would have to specify instructions existing up till the 12th of August, any change of instructions after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, if he can take headphones off again, there is it another important point that I have to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take your headphones off again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me say that your point was important, Your Honour. I didn't mean to say it wasn't. He is saying -- there's confusion now. Is the question what did the MPs on patrol do in addition to what she just read back to him; or is her real question what was the crime police supposed to do? Because now we're talking about different elements of the military police, and to put them all in one umbrella, it seemed that every entry she read said "crime police, turned over to the crime police, crime police released them." So rather than asking a broad question again - I'm reminded to slow down - if we can get more specifics as to -- for the benefit of the witness, as to what specifically the inquiry is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question is clear. My question was as to him, being a member of the military police, what instructions he had received as to how to act in the case of apprehension of perpetrator of suspected person of looting. I mean, it is a simple question. And then if, in fact, there were certain elements of the military police were to act, the witness would certainly offer that explanation. If I were to go into those words, then I would be blamed for loading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just respond. The question was how you were supposed to act in the cases when suspected perpetrators of looting were brought there or apprehended. So brought in to where; and if it's the crime police which we've already established he is not a part of, then, again, I'm just wondering from that question is she asking how once brought in for processing what was supposed to him; or is she asking the broader question, a report comes in about looting, what are you supposed to do. I think those are two separate issues. The latter, the witness has personal knowledge because that was his job. The former, he has already testified he was not a member of the crime police. He may know generally, but -- and if that is the question, the general question of what is the crime police supposed to do, that is fine, too. But the question was what were you supposed to do after they were brought in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, the issue is that it may well be that the witness did not play a role in what should happen after people were brought in. By the way, Mr. Misetic, I understood "to be brought in" as being arrested and taken to a place for further investigation and further processing, so that wasn't the unclear matter. But there was a suggestion that there was a direct involvement of this witness with those persons who were brought in, and that apparently caused concern to Mr. Misetic. Could you, in reformulating your question, could you keep that in mind, and I give you 20 minutes to think about that because we'll have a break first. Ms. Mahindaratne, I'll not announce the break to the witness until after I confess to you that when earlier I said that the reference to the statement of the witness was not clear, that was the reference to when I'm talking about what happened in the previous session, the reference to paragraph 54, that although it was a while ago that you referred to it, you did, and you did it even twice, so to that extent I was mistaken. I, however, got a bit lost because Mr. Misetic then objected; and after that, other things happened, so I lost track of the reference you certainly made and even made twice to paragraph 54. The only thing I hope is that the witness did not loose track together with me. Mr. Dzolic, Mr. Dzolic, we now and then deal with procedural matters and we are asking a lot of your patience, apologies for that, but we have to do it now and then. We'll now first have a break, 20 minutes. We resume quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, I just wish to take you back to what we were discussing; but before we go on, I want to get a minor clarification. Now, those entries I read back to you indicated that the perpetrators were handed over to -- the terms used was "crime police," "criminal investigator," "crime inspector," et cetera. Now, is it correct that these were criminal military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the cases that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my reference, I'm talking about the persons being handed over to crime police or criminal investigator or crime inspector. Is it a reference to criminal military police, that persons were handed over to criminal military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there was also a reference to a term "Runje," R-u-n-j-e. Can you tell Court what that is. It says "crime police, Runje."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: This is probably a member of the criminal military police whose last name is probably Runjic; and then his nickname, which was probably Runje, was indicated there. I don't know what else it could mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't there a location and a place called Runje, R-u-n-j-e, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Object to the leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Let me ask again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where was the crime military police of the Knin military police company located?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: At the company headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was in the Senjak barracks. That's where the Knin company was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you tell us where Senjak barracks was located, in Knin, there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact coordinates, but I will try to explain for the Court to give an approximate description. I don't know how well you know the Knin town, but going from the main street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you could make it short. If you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, isn't the location of the Senjak barracks in evidence 15, 20, or 25 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the criminal military police that these persons were handed over to, were they attached to the Knin military police company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: These were members of the crime police who operated within the company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if the crime police raises a criminal report in relation to a matter, would that be recorded in your duty log-book? I'm saying the crime police attached to your company.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: If the processing was completed on the day when the incident was entered, I suppose that an entry would be made. However, if the duty officer did not receive information as to whether the crime police had raised a criminal report or not, then it would not be entered in the log-book for that day; but, rather, one, two, or ten days later, once the criminal processing was complete and all the parameters required for a criminal report to be raised, then it would be written down in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, now, I read to you a few instances where perpetrators of looting were handed over to criminal military police and were released. Now, in relation to those instances, if a criminal process was initiated and completed, would that be recorded somewhere in this military log-book -- or should that be recorded somewhere in military log-book? Let me rephrase it that way.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer with certainty, but I think that the information as such would probably -- would be entered in the log-book but not on that same day, but maybe ten or 15 days later, once the criminal report was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the military police battalion have access to the log-books of the companies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did the commander of the military police battalion have access to the log-books, this military -- the company log-books? Not only your company, but, generally, could the commander access or did he have access to these log-books?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: He did have access. Whenever they inspected -- they carried out inspection, then a member of the duty service from the battalion would come to check on the work, to monitor or inspect the work of the duty service within the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how often were those inspections carried out?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you for certain. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, let me take to your 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, it's P876.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if could I ask you to look of a paragraph 29, you refer to meetings between the battalion commander, and this is what you say. This is a note official for military police commanders to attend a meeting with the battalion commander, Mihael Budimir, on 12 August 1995 in Knin: "This order was conveyed to me and I can confirm that I attended that meeting, and all the subordinate commanders reported the situation for the last seven days on the ground. I do not recall that the issue of burning, destruction, or looting was discussed at these meetings. The company commanders of 72nd Military Police Battalion met with the battalion commander weekly in Split." Now, at these weekly meetings - now, we've just gone through and seen a few entries in the military police log-book, your company log-book, and you have examined this log-book, Mr. Dzolic - there are a number of entries relating to incidents of looting and burning. Weren't these incidents discussed at the weekly meetings in Split when the company commanders met the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that this was discussed at the collegium in its expanded form for the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it discussed in any other forum that you are aware of, where you were present?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was not present in such meetings where such matters were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may have I document number 456, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, you have referred to this document in paragraph 6 of your 2008 statement -- I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. Mr. Dzolic, I'd like to take to you this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, have page 3 of three of B/C/S; and also in the English version also page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it is reported that the: "Command and control were implemented through the holding of morning meetings of the battalion command and weekly meetings of the battalion command with the platoon and company commanders through the issuing of oral and written orders and visits to and monitoring of units in accordance with the monthly work plans of the battalion command." Now, this is the report on the work of the 72nd Battalion. Now, apart from weekly meetings this is an reference to the daily morning meetings, and I'm not clear exactly what that refers to. Were there daily meetings between the battalion commander and the company commanders of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: There were meetings with the commanders of the local company: The 1st and 2nd Company and the Traffic Company. These commanders attended daily meetings, daily briefings. As for the distant units, such as Zadar, Dubrovnik, Sibenik, Sinj, they were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last few words that the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, could you repeat what you said, the last few words; the interpreter could not catch you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: The commanders of companies of the military police which were not local of the 72nd Battalion, such as Sibenik, Zadar, Sinj, and Dubrovnik, they were present in weekly -- at weekly briefings. They did not come every day to Split for briefings; they came once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "local" can you be -- so that there is no confusion, can you be a little more specific where were these local companies located and which companies are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned local companies, they had their own areas of responsibility over a certain area. I cannot give you with any certainty what the boundaries of those areas of responsibilities were; whereas, these companies were at the seat of the battalion, within the seat of the battalion, and did not have their own area of responsibility, except the 1st Corps of the military police which was within the area of responsibility of the -- of Split town. When I mention locations, I don't want to give the wrong impression, but they were composed -- they were of the same structure, but at the lower level, so at the same structure as the battalion command, and they acted independently in their own areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And would your company be considered one of the local companies that met with the battalion commander daily?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just an objection on foundation, Your Honour. What time-period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During the period 4th August to end of September, was the Knin company -- military police company, did they conduct or did you or the company commander of the Knin military police company conduct daily meetings with the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, just for my information, at that early period of time, until the 12th of August, the battalion command was located where? We could ask the witness. Where was the battalion command located during this first period when you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The battalion command was in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that's what I understood from previous answers. Ms. Mahindaratne, would you be expect someone to travel from Knin to Split on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will clarify and I will ask two further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... well, it is already covered in the statement. I think I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and try to put your questions as focussed as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we have document number 1433, please -- I'm sorry. Before that, before we go off this document, can we just go down to paragraph 6 counting from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is a paragraph here which starts, "I should be mentioned ..." Let me read it out to you, Mr. Dzolic. It says: "It should be mentioned that throughout the year 1995 ..." -- I'm sorry. It's the next paragraph: "When carrying out regular military tasks, most of the problems we encountered arose in searches by units of the Croatian army (incomplete searches, irregularly launched searches, searches for persons not within the competent of the military police)." Are you able to explain what that reference is about?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't say anything about this. I did not compile this document, and I don't know what the person who did compile it wanted to say by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. If you could just go down further on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in B/C/S, if we move to page 5 -- I'm sorry, B/C/S page 6 and English page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Under the heading, "Cooperation of VP units and assessment of cooperation," below the second subparagraph, starting from the third line of that paragraph, it says: "There have been certain problems in the Zadar-Knin police administration due to failure to hold coordination meetings in connection with the behaviour of citizens and members of the HV in the newly liberated areas. The same applies in the Sibenik police administration where there were frequent incidents against members of the HV. The latest example is the behaviour of the said police administration towards the commander of the Split Military District," in the English document going on to the next page, page 6, "Colonel General Ante Gotovina." Are you aware of there being any particular incident or some conflict between the Sibenik police administration and General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have, Mr. Registrar, document number 1433, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I do, because I think you showed it to me at our meeting in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. And you have referred to it in paragraph 31 of your 2008 statement, and this is a document which says: "Criminal reports of the Joint Knin Company for the year of 1995." That's your company, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the report starts only from 5th September. In fact, in paragraph 31, you did indicate that -- some amount of surprise that there were no records before the 5th September. Now, in this document, there are only 25 incidents, criminal reports, raised in the year 1995. Now, being the company commander, are you able to tell Court -- in fact, you did express some amount of surprise. Are you aware that there were more criminal reports raised or more investigations into crime within your company in the year 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. That question should be put to the military crime police. I did not keep records of what number of crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to conduct a comparison of this document with the military police log-book; and in fairness to you, let me take to you a sample, Mr. Dzolic. For the 5th September, there is one criminal report against one person recorded, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to -- Mr. Registrar, if I could have again document 5467, please. That is the log-book, and if we could move to the 5th September entry. That is in B/C/S page 31; and in the English, 7479, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, you can notice -- note there are six incidents of lotting recorded there: At 1045, there is one entry; then at 1300 hours - this is for 5th September - there's a second entry; at 1330, there's a third entry where persons are brought in with looted goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The next page in English. If we could turn to next page, in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At 1500 hours, there's one incident; then 1540 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think B/C/S we are still not on the same page, so next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At 1500 hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. I think you have to go to 7480, page number. Okay. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At 1500 hours, there's a fourth incident reported; 1540, fifth incident; and 1545, sixth incident. So, according to the military police log-book on 5th September, there are six incidents where members of the HV are brought in with looted goods; but according to the report that we just saw, only one criminal report had been raised for 5th September 1995. Now, Mr. Dzolic, can you -- now, you are a military policeman within the 72nd battalion. Can you offer an explanation as to disparity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, as to foundation, continuing objection, and objection as I believe this was at least partially answered previously. [Microphone not activated] ... wishes more on it, I would be willing to say it with the witness taking his headphones off, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, there is foundation. The witness should have knowledge as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, asking him for an explanation -- no. You may put the question to the witness, and we'll see what his answer will be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, can you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to offer an explanation as to why there seems to be, on the face of it, a disparity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection to the characterization in light of the witness's previous testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, Ms. Mahindaratne has put a log to you, where we find some entries on bringing in persons for stolen goods on the 5th of September; and she also has shown you another document, where only one entry is found for the 5th of September in relation to investigation of looting. Do you have an explanation for the difference in numbers? Five in the one; one only in the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no explanation to offer in this respect. I never dealt with the work of the crime police, and I'm not aware of why this has not been registered, whether something was sent for further processing or not. Why this was not entered, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll move on from that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, let me take you to paragraph 11 of your 2008 statement, P876, and there you refer to Major Ivan Juric. You say: "Even to this day, I do not know what his real role was. He seemed to have both a command role and that of a coordinator. According to the organisational structure, Budimir was my superior; although, I think I may have seen an order stating that all the military police units were to be put at the disposal of Major Juric." My question to you is: Did you ever receive any orders from Major Juric? Did you personally receive?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What type of orders were those?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: To get together the forces, to provide security, and to take over the Golubic depot from the members of the Croatian police who were there on a provisional basis. That's an order I can recall at the moment. There were others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any orders relating to crime that was ever issued to you about investigation or arrest of --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any orders issued with regard to investigation or arrest or apprehension or visiting sites of incidents that you received from Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't recall any such order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said there were other orders. Can you recall what type of orders they were or you're not able to recall the other orders that you referred to? You referred to one order.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: There were probably other orders. I can't recall now. For example, securing certain protected facilities such as the one I mentioned just now, the Golubici depot, the Krka military depot, securing other protected facilities in the town of Knin. But so much time has elapsed that I can't recall with precision what these orders were and what exactly they contained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that he was also -- there was a role -- command role and that of a coordinator. Can you explain that term "coordinator." Coordinating what?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: He coordinated the work of the military police and the work of the civilian police. He attended high-level meetings to agree on the work, and then he would provided me with guide-lines as to how the task that had been greed on should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 1629, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also one on your revised list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I will tender this document since it is not included in the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But it's on your revised exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I asked Mr. Registrar to prepare a list, I take it that he would prepare a list of the annexes to the 92 ter statements and not of your revised exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's why I -- those that fall outside 92 ter, Mr. President, I will tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, I appreciate you may not have seen this document, but there is a reference to it and that is why I'm showing you this document. This is a report dated 5th August 1995 submitted by Major Juric. And if we could, if you have time, to just take a look at the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could move, Mr. Registrar, to page 2 of the English; and we remain on page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, do you note the paragraph numbered 1.4. There's a reference to your company, VP company in Knin, and numbers are given. It says: "Led by company commander, Bosko Dzolic has formed a supervisory and control post at the town entry and exit, securing all facilities of special importance, receiving prisoners of war, and preventing violations of public law and order." Now, is that an accurate report of the activities of your company and yourself as of this date?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: This was the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that's correct.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know who -- from where Major Juric would have received this information?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: He should have received this information from me. At that time, I had to report to Commander Budimir and also to Major Juric about the current situation on the ground, about establishing the Knin company, about setting up check-points, and about providing security for facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tendered this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P879, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P879 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, can I take you to paragraph 8 of your 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is P875.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there you say that: "If a member ..." -- you say: "If a member of my company, for example on patrol, saw a crime being committed by a soldier, then the military policeman was to intervene and arrest and take the soldier to the headquarters of the unit of the military police, where he would be handed over to the criminal military police and then taken before an investigative judge who would decide on what course of action was to be taken." Now, were there military crime police units attached to all companies of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there military crime police units attached to all companies of the 72nd Military Police Battalion? Did each company have crime police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, in each event, what does a military police member of military police of a company that does not have crime police attached to that company do when a person is arrested, a perpetrator is arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I wish to clarify here that companies which did not have a crime military police were in the headquarters of the 72nd Battalion, where there was military crime police department dealing with those tasks, and that department was professionally superior to the lower level crime police departments in the companies, those companies that did have a military crime police. And I hope this answers your question. The 1st Company of the military -- general military police which was in the headquarters of the battalion did not have a military crime police department. In accordance with the standard operations procedure listed here in paragraph 8, they would bring that member to the duty service in the battalion, which would then hand over the crime processing of that person to the crime service of the 72nd Battalion of the military police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The military police of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, it says that: "The military policeman who detained the soldier would notify the duty officer who would write a special report based on the original note from the military policeman." Now, when the duty officer writes a special report, to whom were the special reports submitted?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: It would be the duty officer would submit the report, which would be forwarded to the higher command level.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what would the higher command level?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: If it was the company duty service that submitted the report, then it would be to the battalion command. If it was the battalion command, it would be to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was the military commander of the unit to which the -- to which a perpetrator belonged informed when he was arrested and a special report written?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: It's correct that the commander of that unit would also be informed that a member of his unit had perpetrated a crime, so that in accordance with that information and the rules on military discipline, he could take the appropriate action. He could institute disciplinary proceedings against that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. Could you find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I could finish actually within about two minutes, and then my examination-in-chief would be concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will ask only about one or two questions at most, Mr. Dzolic. Now, once an investigative process was completed or a member of the HV was charged or a trial was completed, was the unit commander of the unit to which a person belonged informed of the investigative process or what the outcome had been?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, whether the military court sent information on its judgement concerning the soldier of the unit against whom the proceedings had been held before the military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If the military police had raised a criminal report or charges had been preferred, would that fact be informed to the unit commander by the military police? I'm not talking about the courts --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If, for instance, the military police investigated and, you know, charges were preferred or, say, a person was sent --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I withdraw that question, Mr. President. I will conclude my examination-in-chief at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Dzolic, tomorrow, you will be cross-examined by Defence counsel, and there may be questions or more questions from the Bench as well. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is the testimony you gave already or whether it is the testimony you still are about to give. I, first, would like to -- we'd like to see you back at 9.00 tomorrow, but I'd already ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the parties what their estimates are as far as time for cross-examination is concerned. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going first with this witness with the agreement of my learned friends. I think I will be about three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three hours. And, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will go second, Your Honour, and I think I could stay within two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I also would stay within two hours, hopefully less in light of what I expect in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That gives at least an impression. As always, the Chamber will -- it is rather useless to say that this time is granted or not granted. The Chamber will carefully observe how cross-examination goes, and then see whether to grant more time or whether it finds reasons to say that you should conclude quicker than you had in mind. We adjourn until tomorrow, the 18th of September, 9.00, in this same courtroom, number III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
